newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila MPs to visit disputed S.China Sea area.
newsitem.headline: Manila MPs to visit disputed S.China Sea area.

text.p: At least four Philippine legislators plan to sail to the disputed Scarborough shoal in the South China Sea early on Saturday morning, congressional officials said on Friday.

The shoal recently sparked a diplomatic row between Manila and Beijing when a group of Filipino fishermen raised a Philippine flag and removed Chinese markers on the isle, 120 miles off Subic, north of Manila.
Beijing says all the islands in the South China Sea historically belong to China.
Scarborough is not part of the Spratly islands in the South China Sea, a cluster of potentially oil-rich isles and reefs that are claimed by six Asian countries.

Roger Rigor, committee secretary of the House committee on national defence, said the congressmen and a media contingent would leave Subic free port at 11:00 p.m. (1500 GMT) on Friday in a naval patrol craft for the approximately five-hour boat ride to the shoal.
"This is in reaction to the diplomatic protest of China against the Philippines. The visit is for the congressmen to get more or less familiarised with the island," Rigor told Reuters.

On Tuesday, China said the raising of a Philippine flag on the isle was a "serious violation" of sovereignty and warned that a repeat would strain relations. Beijing sent Manila a diplomatic note on May 9.
Rigor said the group would just have a look around the island and be briefed by a Naval officer. They are scheduled to leave at about 6:00 a.m. (2200 GMT).

A congressional aide said the lawmakers were likely to draft a resolution in response to the diplomatic note after they return to Manila. He said the group did not expect any blockade from the Chinese navy for their dawn visit.

Among the lawmakers who are set to join the trip were Roque Ablan, chairman of the House committee on inter-parliamentary relations and diplomacy; Jose Yap, chairman of the House committee on national defence; Jaime Lopez, chairman of the House committee on foreign affairs; and Junie Cua.
None of the congressmen were available for comment. Chinese embassy officials in Manila were also unavailable.
